name: Electroacupuncture

lead: Electroacupuncture is acupuncture with a mild electric current run between pairs of inserted needles. People use it mainly for pain, such as joint pain, which can support training and recovery, and some cosmetic clinics offer needle-based facial treatments.

Research is largest for pain. A 2024 network meta-analysis of 80 knee osteoarthritis trials reported that acupuncture, including electroacupuncture, may reduce pain, but graded the certainty as very low compared with sham. Cosmetic uses have far less published research.

paras: A trained practitioner inserts needles at selected points and connects pairs to a stimulator that delivers low-frequency current for a session, with treatment typically spread over several visits. Laboratory work has examined lower frequencies of 2 to 10 Hz versus 100 Hz for pain.

Risks include bruising, soreness and infection from needles, and the current is a consideration for people with implanted electronic devices. Practitioner choice and clean technique are the main safety factors.

angle.text: Athletes and lifters use it for joint and muscle pain so they can keep training. Some clinics also offer it on the face for skin appearance, but trials focus on pain conditions.

lead: Electroacupuncture is a form of acupuncture in which a small electric current is passed between pairs of acupuncture needles [1]. Practitioners use it mainly for pain and some digestive or other complaints.

Its route to appearance is mostly indirect: pain relief and recovery support steady training, and some beauty clinics offer needle-based facial treatments marketed for skin tone and tightness. Published research centres on pain; the Wikipedia article reviews trials in rheumatoid arthritis and pregnancy nausea without mentioning cosmetic use [1].
infobox: Offered by some clinics; little published research

paras: In electroacupuncture, needles are inserted as in conventional acupuncture and then linked in pairs to a device delivering a small current [1]. Laboratory studies report that it engages the nervous system differently in healthy and painful states and may inhibit inflammatory and neuropathic pain more effectively at 2 to 10 Hz than at 100 Hz [2].
A 2014 review in Anesthesiology describes preclinical findings that electroacupuncture activates opioids and other bioactive chemicals through peripheral, spinal and supraspinal mechanisms [2].

A 2024 systematic review and network meta-analysis of 80 trials (9,933 participants) in knee osteoarthritis included manual acupuncture and electroacupuncture. It found that acupuncture may reduce pain compared with sham, with very low certainty evidence, and explored differences by type, dose and follow-up [3]. A 2024 network meta-analysis of 45 trials in chronic constipation compared acupuncture with drugs, probiotics, fibre and fecal transplant [4], and a 2024 meta-analysis examined acupuncture for cancer pain [5]. A Cochrane review found no evidence to recommend acupuncture or electroacupuncture for rheumatoid arthritis, and a 2016 meta-analysis of nausea and vomiting in pregnancy was inconclusive [1]. No trials in the cited literature examine electroacupuncture for facial appearance.
